questions.stem: Given the phasor representation of a signal V = 10∠30° V, what is the corresponding time-domain waveform in volts (V)?
questions.solution: The phasor V = 10∠30° represents a sinusoidal waveform in the complex form. To convert it to the time domain, we use Euler's formula: e^(jθ) = cos(θ) + jsin(θ). In this case, V = 10e^(j30°). The real part of the phasor gives the cosine function and the imaginary part gives the sine function. So, the time-domain waveform is V(t) = 10cos(ωt) * cos(30°) + j10sin(ωt) * sin(30°). Since cos(30°) = √3/2 and sin(30°) = 1/2, we get V(t) = 5√3cos(ωt) + 5sin(ωt). However, the question asks for the waveform in terms of sine only. To convert the cosine term to sine, we use the identity cos(θ) = sin(90° - θ): V(t) = 5sin(90° - 30°) + 5sin(ωt) = 5sin(60°) + 5sin(ωt). Since sin(60°) = √3/2, the final waveform is V(t) = 10sin(ωt + 30°).
questions.explanation: The correct answer uses the Euler's formula to convert the phasor to a time-domain sine wave with the appropriate phase shift.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to directly use the cosine function from the phasor without considering the conversion to sine. Choice A represents this error by using cos(ωt - 30°) instead of the correct sine form.

questions.stem: What is the time-domain waveform for the phasor I = 8∠-45° A, expressed in amperes (A)?
questions.solution: Similar to the previous question, we use Euler's formula to convert the phasor to the time domain: e^(jθ) = cos(θ) + jsin(θ). In this case, I = 8e^(-j45°). The imaginary part of the phasor gives the sine function. So, the time-domain waveform is I(t) = 8sin(-ωt) * sin(-45°) - 8cos(-ωt) * cos(-45°). Since sin(-θ) = -sin(θ) and cos(-θ) = cos(θ), we get I(t) = -8sin(ωt) * sin(45°) + 8cos(ωt) * cos(45°). Using the values for sin(45°) and cos(45°), which are both √2/2, we have I(t) = -4√2sin(ωt) + 4√2cos(ωt). To express this in terms of a single sine function, we use the sum- to-product identity: sinα + sinβ = 2sin((α+β)/2)cos((α-β)/2). In our case, α = ωt and β = 90°. So, I(t) = 4√2sin((ωt + 90°)/2)cos((ωt - 90°)/2). Since cos(45°) = √2/2, the final waveform is I(t) = 8sin(ωt + 135°).
questions.explanation: The correct answer correctly converts the phasor to a time-domain sine wave with the appropriate phase shift.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake is to use the cosine function directly from the phasor without considering the conversion to sine. Choice B represents this error by using cos(ωt - 90°) instead of the correct sine form.

So, V(t) = 6sin((ωt - 180°)/2)cos((ωt + 180°)/2). Since cos(90°) = 0, the final waveform is V(t) = 6sin(ωt + 120°).

questions.solution: Using Euler's formula, we have e^(jθ) = cos(θ) + jsin(θ). For the phasor V = 2∠-60°, the imaginary part gives the sine function. So, the time-domain waveform is V(t) = 2sin(-ωt) * sin(-60°) - 2cos(-ωt) * cos(-60°). Since sin(-θ) = -sin(θ) and cos(-θ) = cos(θ), we get V(t) = -2sin(ωt) * (-1/2) + 2cos(ωt) * (√3/2). This simplifies to V(t) = √3cos(ωt) + sin(ωt). To express this in terms of a single cosine function, we use the sum- to-product identity: cosα + cosβ = 2cos((α+β)/2)cos((α-β)/2). In our case, α = ωt and β = 60°. So, V(t) = 2cos((ωt + 60°)/2)cos((ωt - 60°)/2). Since cos(30°) = √3/2, the final waveform is V(t) = √3cos(ωt + 120°).
